questions.question: What core problems associated with traditional manual attendance and early biometric systems prompted you to propose this face recognition attendance solution?
expected_points: Manual roll calls waste around 10 minutes of lecture time and suffer from proxy attendance.
RFID cards can be shared between students, still permitting proxy attendance.
Fingerprint scanners eliminate card sharing but cause bottlenecks and queues since only one student can be scanned at a time.

questions.question: Why did you choose a deep learning embedding approach over traditional computer vision techniques like Haar cascades for face recognition?
expected_points: Haar cascades were fast but proved inaccurate under poor lighting conditions.
Deep learning models map faces to a 128-dimensional embedding where faces of the same person are clustered close together.
FaceNet paired with MTCNN exhibits over 99% accuracy on the LFW benchmark and runs in real time on a mid-range GPU.

questions.question: Explain the three-tier architecture of your system and how data flows from the classroom to the final attendance record.
expected_points: Capture tier runs on a classroom computer with a 1080p camera sending one frame every two seconds.
Application tier is a Python Flask REST API performing face detection with MTCNN and computing FaceNet embeddings.
Data tier is a MySQL database storing student, course, session, and attendance information.

questions.question: How does the system prevent spoofing attempts, such as a student holding up a photograph or phone screen of someone else?
expected_points: A liveness detection mechanism tracks eye blinking across consecutive frames to detect live presence.
A student must be recognised across at least three separate frames within the first fifteen minutes rather than just a single momentary snapshot.

questions.question: Describe the student enrollment process: what inputs are gathered, how is the face template generated, and how are raw images handled?
expected_points: Twenty images per student are captured from different angles during enrollment.
Each image is aligned, resized to 160x160 pixels, and processed through the embedding model.
The average embedding is calculated and saved as the student's template.
Raw face images are permanently deleted post-enrollment to protect privacy.

questions.question: What measures have you implemented to safeguard student biometric data and comply with privacy considerations?
expected_points: Raw face images are deleted immediately after enrollment so that no photographs are retained.
Biometric face embeddings are kept in a separate table and encrypted with AES-256.
Only the API service account is authorized to read the stored face embeddings.

questions.question: Explain the database schema design: which tables exist, and what database optimization was done to ensure fast report generation?
expected_points: There are five main tables: students, courses, enrollments, lecture_sessions, and attendance (plus face_embeddings).
The attendance table references student_id and session_id and logs first seen time and count of recognised frames.
Indexes on student_id and session_id maintain query execution times below 100 milliseconds across a full semester.

questions.question: How did you determine the similarity threshold of 0.75, and what were the resulting error rates on your validation set?
expected_points: Tuned empirically using a validation set comprising 40 students.
A threshold of 0.75 balanced identification rates by achieving a False Acceptance Rate (FAR) of 0.5%.
It maintained a False Rejection Rate (FRR) of 3%.

questions.question: Looking at the matching logic implemented in face_matcher.py, how are face embeddings compared against enrolled templates and matched to an identity?
expected_points: Uses cosine similarity computed as the dot product divided by the product of the L2 norms of the vectors.
Iterates over enrolled templates and identifies the student ID with the highest similarity score exceeding the 0.75 threshold.
Returns None if no enrolled student exceeds the 0.75 similarity threshold.

questions.question: According to update_attendance in face_matcher.py, what is the exact rule for marking a student present in a session?
expected_points: The system increments a frame count for the identified student ID each time they are matched.
The student is marked present only when their recognition count reaches at least MIN_FRAMES_FOR_PRESENT (3 frames).
These frames must occur during the first fifteen minutes of the lecture session.

questions.question: How did you test your system prior to classroom deployment, and what were the key performance metrics achieved during the pilot trial?
expected_points: Unit tests validated individual API endpoints and face-matching logic.
Integration tests replayed recorded classroom video feeds through the complete pipeline.
Pilot deployment evaluated 3 classes of 45 students over two weeks, attaining 96.8% accuracy compared to manual roll call and completing attendance in an average of 40 seconds.

questions.question: What primary failure modes or recognition errors were encountered during classroom testing, and how were they mitigated?
expected_points: Errors primarily resulted from students wearing face masks or sitting in the back row under poor lighting conditions.
Deploying a second camera positioned at the back of the classroom cut these recognition errors in half.

questions.question: To what extent did the deployed system meet the primary project objectives you set out in the beginning?
expected_points: Attendance time was reduced from approximately 10 minutes to under 1 minute (averaging 40 seconds in trials).
Proxy attendance was eliminated during the pilot classes.
Real-time visibility was provided via a teacher dashboard while securing biometric data.

questions.question: What future extensions and technical improvements are planned to address the shortcomings identified during the pilot evaluation?
expected_points: Developing masked face recognition to handle students wearing masks.
Building a dedicated mobile application for teachers.
Integrating the system directly with the university learning management system (LMS).

questions.question: What trade-offs were made regarding the camera capture rate and input resolution between hardware demands and system responsiveness?
expected_points: Frames were captured at 1080p to provide sufficient resolution for face detection in a classroom setting.
The capture rate was limited to one frame every two seconds rather than a high-fps stream to reduce network overhead and API processing load on the mid-range GPU.
Captured faces were cropped and downscaled to 160x160 before embedding computation.
